Summary

NAM (Navigation Assistant of Mars) is a navigation and survival assistant for Mars. It combines a 3D CesiumJS globe with a Python FastAPI backend that puts real NASA science data MOLA terrain, IAU landform names, SWIM water-ice proxy, RAD radiation levels, and known lava-tube shelters behind a single API.

Users can search any of 112 named Martian locations, sample terrain elevation and slope at any point, plan routes between two spots with an A* pathfinder that avoids steep or rough ground, check the nearest shelter, and simulate hazards like dust storms and solar particle events. A natural-language assistant ties it together you can ask "Take me to Olympus Mons" or "Plan a safe route from Jezero to Nili Patera" and get a real answer with distance, slope, and exposure estimate.

It addresses the challenge by turning Mars from a static map into a navigable, hazard-aware place useful for future mission planners, crews, and students. It matters because surviving on Mars will require decisions grounded in real data, and NAM shows how those decisions can be both practical and scientifically honest.

Project Details — NAM (Navigation Assistant of Mars)

What it does / How it works

NAM is a planetary-scale navigation and survival assistant for Mars. It pairs a CesiumJS 3D globe (the v1 frontend, NAM.html) with a purpose-built FastAPI backend that layers real NASA science data and a routing/planning engine on top of the imagery.

A user opens the globe, searches for any of 102 IAU-named Martian landforms or 13

Every value carries its source and uncertainty, so the tool never passes off an estimate as a measurement.mission landing sites, and can then:

  • Sample terrain at any lat/lon through bilinear interpolation of the MOLA MEGDR elevation grid (1440×720, 4 pixels per degree) plus a MOLA-derived roughness grid
  • Every value carries its source and uncertainty, so the tool never passes off an estimate as a measurement.(360×180).
  • Analyze hazards at a point: slope estimate, terrain roughness, an aggregated hazard score, and a sea-level-style atmospheric pressure estimate derived from elevation.
  • Plan traverses with an A* router that operates on the MOLA grid and supports three presets (balanced / terrain-avoiding / speed-priority), returning a polyline, total distance, accumulated elevation gain/loss, and per-segment slope.
  • Query the environment: 12 candidate shelter sites (anchored to Cushing 2007 lava-tube skylights), a proxy subsurface water-ice inventory based on SWIM/Morgan 2021, and a radiation exposure model anchored to the MSL RAD surface baseline of ~0.21 mSv/day (Hassler 2014) with SEP event scaling (Guo 2018).
  • Simulate threats: local, regional, and global (MY34-class) dust storms, plus M/X-class Solar Energetic Particle events, with estimated dosages and shelter recommendations.
  • Walk View: a first-person rover-perspective layer at 1.7 m eye height, with a 1 km terrain-height grid and pre-cached POV thumbnails from Perseverance, Curiosity, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight imagery.
  • Ask the assistant in natural language ("Take me to Olympus Mons", "Plan a route from Jezero to Nili Patera avoiding slopes over 15°", "Where's the nearest shelter from 18°N 77°E?"). The assistant exposes 25 tools, an intent router, and an SSE chat channel that is OpenAI-compatible so it can be wired to a real LLM later.

All geospatial, environmental, and health-related values carry a provenance block (source, model, uncertainty note, and a link back to the originating dataset or paper). Simulated/derived values are explicitly tagged [SIM] so no figure is mistaken for measured truth.

Benefits

  • One surface for many datasets: MOLA topography, roughness, IAU gazetteer, SWIM water-ice proxy, RAD radiation, lava-tube shelters, mission imagery — usually scattered across PDS, USGS, and OpenPlanetaryMap — unified behind a single REST + WebSocket API.
  • Decision-ready output: routes come with distance, slope, elevation profile, and exposure estimate; shelter queries come back with reasoning; storms come with recommended actions.
  • Honest by design: every derived number says where it came from and what it is not (e.g., the radiation model is an exposure scaling, not a particle transport calculation; SWIM water-ice is a coarse regional proxy, not a drill-target cert).
  • Pluggable: tile proxy, OpenAI-compatible chat, REST + WS contracts mean the UI team can build against a documented surface and swap in better data sources without rewriting the frontend.

Intended impact

Give a future Mars crew, a mission planner, or a classroom a tool that turns Mars from a wallpaper image into a navigable, hazard-aware, science-anchored place — while keeping every assertion traceable to a real source. It is a reference for how an "Interplanetary Survival Guide" can be both useful and scientifically honest.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, NumPy, httpx, websockets.
  • Frontend: CesiumJS, vanilla JS (single-file HTML), embedded MOLA terrain.
  • Data: NASA PDS MOLA MEGDR (elevation + roughness), USGS SIM 3292 and IAU Gazetteer (nomenclature/missions), OpenPlanetaryMap basemap tiles, NASA/JPL rover imagery for Walk View POVs.
  • Science anchors: Hassler 2014 (RAD), Guo 2018 (SEP), Montabone 2015 (dust storms), Morgan 2021 (SWIM), Cushing 2007 (lava-tube skylights).
  • Infra: Docker, docker-compose, pytest (15 unit tests + 35 HTTP smoke tests), a one-shot demo scenario (Jezero X-class SEP evacuation drill).
  • Distribution: a 2.1 MB backend zip with API.md as the single source of truth for the UI team.

How the project is creative

  • Provenance as a first-class field, not a footnote — every number carries its source, model, and uncertainty, so the tool never silently passes off an estimate as a measurement.
  • Walk View bridges orbital CesiumJS imagery with rover-perspective ground truth at eye height, giving a "Martian Street View" feel without inventing data.
  • Natural-language control of the globe through 25 documented assistant tools and an intent router, with an SSE chat channel that is OpenAI-compatible for a later real LLM swap.
  • End-to-end simulation scenarios, e.g. an X-class SEP event over Jezero → nearest shelter → terrain-avoiding route → dose estimate, all in one call chain.

Factors the team considered

  • One-day build window: scope was forced to be sharp — a complete backend contract over a half-built UI.
  • Scientific honesty: MOLA was extracted from the v1 file rather than re-downloaded from PDS; SWIM is a coarse proxy; the radiation model is a scaling, not transport — all disclosed.
  • Team split: UI and backend
  • Coordinate conventions: latitude −90..90 (south negative), longitude 0..360 east, auto-normalized, to avoid the common ±180 / 0..360 mismatches in Mars data.
  • Graceful degradation: the tile proxy honestly returns 503 + the upstream source link when OpenPlanetaryMap is unreachable, instead of serving blank tiles.
